content_voiceover: This diagram illustrates the biological mechanisms driving cancer associated thrombosis, a topic that ties together tumor biology and coagulation physiology. The tumor drives thrombosis through multiple parallel pathways. First, tumor cells release extracellular vesicles bearing tissue factor, which directly activate the extrinsic coagulation pathway to generate fibrin. Tumor cells also shed polyphosphate containing vesicles that activate Factor twelve, feeding into fibrin formation through the intrinsic pathway. The tumor also increases PAI one, plasminogen activator inhibitor one, which suppresses fibrinolysis, meaning clots that do form are degraded more slowly. On the cellular side, tumor cells express podoplanin, PDPN, which activates platelets directly, and platelet activation contributes to thrombus formation. Tumor cells also recruit and activate neutrophils, which release neutrophil extracellular traps, or NETs, a scaffold that promotes clot formation. Finally, tumor cells activate monocytes to express tissue factor, which again drives fibrin generation. All of these pathways converge on the same endpoint, venous thrombosis. Understanding this multi-hit mechanism helps explain why cancer patients are in a profoundly hypercoagulable state and why anticoagulant prophylaxis is often considered in high risk patients.
keypoints: Tumor-derived tissue factor bearing vesicles directly trigger fibrin formation
Polyphosphate vesicles activate Factor twelve to promote clotting
Tumor upregulates PAI one, impairing fibrinolysis
Podoplanin activates platelets, and tumor cells trigger NETs from neutrophils
Monocyte tissue factor expression is another convergent pathway to fibrin
keypoint_voiceover: Cancer promotes thrombosis through multiple converging mechanisms, tissue factor bearing vesicles, Factor twelve activation, impaired fibrinolysis via PAI one, platelet activation, neutrophil extracellular traps, and monocyte tissue factor expression.
